summary: Describes OAKLEY, a protocol in which two authenticated parties agree on shared secret keying material using the Diffie-Hellman key exchange as its basic mechanism. It influenced the design of IKE. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: OAKLEY lets two parties agree on secret keying material using a Diffie-Hellman exchange. It also provides ways to authenticate the parties and optionally protect identities or add other key-management features.

questions: what is the oakley key determination protocol
how does oakley relate to isakmp and ike
subtitle: A Diffie-Hellman protocol for two authenticated parties to establish shared keying material.

tldr.problem: Two parties need a way to establish secret keys and authenticate each other across a network.
tldr.mechanism: OAKLEY combines Diffie-Hellman, authentication, algorithm negotiation, cookies, and optional identity protection or forward secrecy.
tldr.outcome: The Informational RFC describes a protocol designed to work with ISAKMP; the exact mapping to ISAKMP fields was left to a separate document.

sections.title: Purpose of OAKLEY
sections.content:
OAKLEY is a protocol for two authenticated parties to agree on shared secret keying material. Its basic mechanism is Diffie-Hellman, which lets the parties compute a shared value without sending that value itself.

The RFC adds ways to validate addresses before expensive calculations, negotiate supporting algorithms, and choose standard or user-defined groups. It also describes perfect forward secrecy, key updates, and use of keys distributed out of band.
sections.plainLanguage: OAKLEY helps two parties create a shared secret over a network. It also lets them check identities and choose how the exchange is protected.

sections.title: Cookies, Identifiers, and Key Material
sections.content:
Each party contributes a 64-bit pseudo-random cookie. The cookies provide a weak check that a sender can receive replies at its address and can let a responder delay expensive work. Together, the two cookies form the key identifier, or KEYID.

The secret keying material named by the KEYID is called sKEYID and is never transmitted. Messages can also contain group choices, Diffie-Hellman values, algorithm offers, identities, and nonces. A good random-number generator is required by the protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Each side sends a cookie that helps identify the exchange and check reachability. The shared secret is computed by both sides and never sent in a message.

sections.title: The Key Exchange
sections.content:
An exchange has three components: cookie handling, an optional Diffie-Hellman exchange, and authentication. The parties can combine optional features such as stateless cookies, identity secrecy, and perfect forward secrecy. With some options omitted, the RFC shows an exchange completed in three messages.

The initiator offers information and algorithms; the responder may accept all, some, or none of the offer. The parties authenticate the exchange and derive keying material from the Diffie-Hellman value, nonces, and cookies. The initiator retransmits if the exchange does not finish in time.
sections.plainLanguage: The parties exchange cookies, key-exchange values, and authentication data. They can include more steps for extra protections, or use a shorter exchange when those protections are not needed.

sections.title: Identities and Authentication Methods
sections.content:
The initiator can provide its claimed identity and the responder's requested identity. If neither is supplied, the identities are taken from the IP header addresses. The responder may return a different identity, which the initiator can accept by continuing or reject by stopping.

Authentication can use a pre-shared key, public-key encryption, or signatures. The RFC requires support for pre-shared keys and DNS public-key records, while other certificate and key options are optional. Authentication must validate the Diffie-Hellman values as part of binding them to the parties.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trusting the new key, each party checks who the other party claims to be. They can use a previously shared secret or public-key information.

sections.title: Private Groups and Additional Keys
sections.content:
Once an authenticated key exists, OAKLEY can establish a private Diffie-Hellman group, derive new keys using a hash function, or transfer externally generated keying material. A private group has a name shared by the two parties and a description protected by an existing key.

These features reuse authenticated state instead of repeating every part of a full exchange. The RFC requires the key used to protect an externally generated key to be at least as strong as that external key.
sections.plainLanguage: An existing authenticated key can help create additional keys or protect a new group description. Any key used to protect another key must be strong enough for that job.
